title: Joseph in Potiphar's House
summary: Sold as a slave in Egypt, Joseph rises to manage the household of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, because the LORD is with him and blesses the house for his sake. Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce him, and when he flees she accuses him of assault. Joseph is thrown into the king's prison, where the LORD is still with him and he is soon put in charge again.
story: Chapter 37 ended with Joseph sold into Egypt, and chapter 38 stepped aside to follow Judah. Now the story returns to Joseph, picking up the thread with the same fact: he has been brought down to Egypt and sold. From here to the end of Genesis the family's future will be decided in Egypt, and this chapter sets the pattern for Joseph's years there: descent, faithfulness, favor, and a further descent, all under the repeated statement that the LORD was with him. The contrast with the chapter before is deliberate. Judah, a free man among his own, went after a woman he took for a prostitute; Joseph, a slave far from home, refuses his master's wife at great cost. The prison where he ends up is where he will meet Pharaoh's officials in chapter 40, the door through which he will eventually reach Pharaoh himself.
historical:
Genesis does not name the Pharaoh, and the date of Joseph's time in Egypt depends on how one dates the patriarchs and the exodus. Those who take the Bible's numbers at face value often place Joseph in Egypt's Middle Kingdom, early in the second millennium BC; others connect him with the period when Semitic rulers, the Hyksos, held northern Egypt (about 1650 to 1550 BC); still others regard the story as shaped much later. What is clear is that people from Canaan and Syria did live and work in Egypt in the second millennium BC. An Egyptian document known as Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446, from about the eighteenth century BC, lists household servants in an Egyptian estate, and a good number of them carry Semitic names.

Potiphar is called a saris of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. The first title literally can mean eunuch, but it was also used for court officials in general, and since Potiphar has a wife, most translations render it "officer". The second title, literally chief of the butchers or slaughterers, probably marks him as head of the royal bodyguard or of those who carried out the king's sentences, which fits the prison connected to his office.
cultural:
Joseph's position, a household slave put in charge of everything, has parallels across the ancient Near East, where trusted slaves could manage estates for their owners. Verse 6 says Potiphar concerned himself with nothing "except the food he ate", which may mean he kept only his own table in his hands, possibly because Egyptians would not eat with foreigners (43:32). Joseph's title "this Hebrew" in the wife's mouth is an ethnic label with contempt in it: she turns the household servants against him as an outsider and blames her husband for bringing him ("has been brought to us"). In a society where a slave's word counted for little against his mistress's, Joseph had no defense.

Egyptian literature itself contains a story with a similar shape. The Tale of Two Brothers, preserved in a papyrus from about 1200 BC, tells of a married woman who tries to seduce her husband's younger brother, is refused, and then accuses him falsely. The parallel shows that the situation was a familiar one in that world. The differences matter too: in Genesis the refusal is grounded in loyalty to a master and, above all, in not sinning against God.
literary: The chapter is framed by a repeated refrain: "the LORD was with Joseph" (verse 2), "the LORD was with him" (verse 3), and again at the end (verses 21 and 23). The name LORD (Yahweh), rare in the Joseph story, clusters here, framing the scene of temptation between two statements of God's presence. Words for hand and for leaving run through the story: Potiphar leaves everything in Joseph's hand, and Joseph leaves his cloak in the woman's hand and runs. The cloak itself recalls chapter 37, where a garment was also used to deceive a father about Joseph. The wife tells her story twice, once to the servants and once to her husband, and each version shifts the blame a little further. The chapter ends almost where it began: Joseph lower than before, yet trusted with everything, because God is with him.

outline.t: The LORD blesses Potiphar's house through Joseph
Joseph refuses his master's wife day after day
The cloak and the false accusation
The LORD is with Joseph in prison

doctrines.note: God's presence does not keep Joseph from slavery, slander, or prison, but it goes with him into each of them. The chapter teaches that God's favor and human suffering can exist at the same time, and that God works through setbacks toward purposes not yet visible (see 50:20).

Joseph calls adultery "such a great evil" and a sin "against God", not only against his master. His integrity is shaped by his relation to God, even in a land where no one from his family is watching.
God promised Abraham that through his family others would be blessed (12:3). Here an Egyptian household is blessed "on account of" Joseph, a small early fulfillment of that promise.

words.note: Tsalach, to prosper or succeed. The verb frames the chapter: Joseph becomes "a successful man" in verse 2 and the LORD gives him "success in whatever he did" in verse 23. Success here is not wealth or freedom, since Joseph is a slave and then a prisoner; it is God making his work fruitful wherever he is placed.

Chata, to sin, literally to miss a mark. Joseph's question, "how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?", shows that he understands wrongdoing first in relation to God. The same understanding lies behind David's confession in Psalm 51:4.

Chesed, steadfast love or loyal kindness, a central word in the Old Testament for the faithful love God shows within a relationship he has committed himself to. The BSB renders it "kindness" in verse 21: in prison, when every human loyalty has failed Joseph, God's loyalty has not.

Tsachaq, to laugh, and in some forms to play, jest, or mock. The wife says Joseph was brought "to make sport of us", a charge with sexual overtones. The same root gives Isaac his name (laughter) and appears in 26:8 of Isaac caressing Rebekah, so the word can carry both mockery and intimacy.

christ: Joseph is one of the Old Testament's clearest examples of the righteous sufferer: a man who does right and suffers for it, whom God vindicates and exalts in the end, and through whom many are saved. The New Testament doesn't call Joseph a type of Christ in so many words, though Stephen's speech in Acts 7:9-10 retells his story as one in which the patriarchs were jealous and sold him, "But God was with him" and rescued him. The pattern of betrayal, false accusation, descent, and exaltation is the pattern Jesus fulfills most fully. Hebrews 4:15 speaks of a high priest who has been tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, and Peter tells believers who suffer unjustly to look to Christ, who entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:21-23). Joseph's story is a thematic foreshadowing, not a prediction, but it is part of the long preparation for a Messiah who is innocent, condemned, and raised up.

hard.q: If the LORD was with Joseph, why did Joseph end up in prison for doing the right thing?
hard.a:
The chapter refuses to treat God's presence as a guarantee of good outcomes in the short run. Joseph is faithful and is punished for it. Some readers find this troubling, and the Bible does not hide the tension: the Psalms and Job ask the same question. The narrative's answer comes in stages. First, God's presence is real in the prison itself, where Joseph receives kindness and responsibility. Second, the prison becomes the place where he meets the people who will bring him to Pharaoh, so the injustice becomes part of the road God uses. Third, the whole story is interpreted at its end, when Joseph tells his brothers that what they meant for evil God meant for good (50:20). That answer does not make the injustice good, and the text never says Potiphar's wife was right. It says that God is not defeated by it.

Some readers also wonder why Potiphar imprisoned rather than executed Joseph, since an accusation like this could carry a death sentence. The text doesn't explain, and suggestions (that Potiphar doubted his wife, or that the prison was simply his own jurisdiction) remain guesses.

questions: Joseph describes resisting temptation as refusing to sin against God, not only against Potiphar. How does that change how you think about private choices?
The chapter says the LORD was with Joseph both when he prospered and when he was in prison. Where have you been tempted to read hardship as a sign of God's absence?
Joseph fled rather than argued. What situations in your life call for leaving rather than trying to stand your ground?
